claims.text: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles qualify as high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles exhibit a single-phase or near-homogeneous solid-solution state at room temperature.
In situ aberration-corrected HRTEM equipped with a heating stage can resolve atomic-scale structural evolution in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at high temperature.
Such in situ AC-HRTEM observations can directly validate thermodynamic contributions to enhanced thermal stability.
Heating should be performed under controlled vacuum or inert atmosphere at temperatures representative of high-temperature applications.
The relevant structural mediators include atomic lattice arrangements, ordering, dislocation activity, and phase boundaries.
Thermal energy induces atomic diffusion and rearrangement in the nanoparticles.
Thermally induced rearrangements can produce ordering or disordering transitions.
Thermally induced rearrangements can produce minor phase segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Atomic-scale diffusion, ordering, and segregation mediate the overall thermal stability predicted by thermodynamic models.
Heating will produce observable changes in lattice symmetry, ordered clusters, or diffusion-mediated surface reconstruction.
The observed atomic rearrangements will correlate with theoretically predicted enhanced thermal stability.
Room-temperature imaging will show a homogeneous distribution of the alloying elements.
Electron-beam irradiation may itself induce structural changes in the nanoparticles.
Reproducibility and separation from irradiation artifacts are required to attribute observed changes to thermal annealing.
Selected-area electron diffraction can be used to detect changes in lattice symmetry during heating.
The nature and onset temperature of the thermally induced transitions are uncertain.
A lack of detectable atomic-scale structural changes over the expected temperature range would falsify the claim that AC-HRTEM can validate enhanced thermal stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis concerns enhanced thermal stability, but the falsification rule treats the absence of structural change as disconfirming. Structural invariance during heating could instead be evidence of thermal stability, and a null sample response would not by itself falsify the resolving capability of AC-HRTEM.
